History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
• 32-year-old man with 6-week history of intermittent unilateral (left) hearing loss, tinnitus, and mild disequilibrium; video visit arranged primarily to organise face-to-face otoscopic examination to rule out cerumen impaction and other external/middle-ear pathology.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “can’t hear as well as I used to” in left ear.  
• Onset/duration – Began ~6 weeks ago; intermittent.  
• Character/progression – Fluctuating muffled hearing in left ear; right ear normal.  
• Associated symptoms  
  – Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in left ear; often less noticeable when TV/music playing.  
  – Occasional mild dizziness/off-balance sensation (not true vertigo; no nausea).  
• Pertinent negatives – No ear pain, no otorrhoea, no pruritus, no fever, no chest pain, no palpitations.  
• Prior similar episode – Brief 2-day episode of hearing difficulty about 1 year ago, resolved spontaneously.  
• Exposures – Denies cotton-bud use.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions documented.  
• Prior brief unilateral hearing difficulty (see History).

Medications:
• None reported (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
• None reported.

Social History:
• Privacy confirmed for call.  
• Smoking, alcohol, occupation, and noise exposure not discussed.  

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals – Not recorded.  
• General/ENT/Neurologic examination – Not performed (video visit).

Investigations:
• None to date.  
• Plan: Schedule face-to-face clinic visit within 4-5 days for otoscopic examination to assess for cerumen impaction or other ear pathology.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
Unilateral (left) fluctuating hearing loss with tinnitus; most likely conductive cause such as cerumen impaction, but inner-ear conditions remain in differential.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Cerumen impaction – gradual unilateral loss, tinnitus; easy to confirm with otoscopy.  
2. Menière’s disease – hearing loss + tinnitus + disequilibrium; vertigo not classic.  
3. Serous otitis media / Eustachian-tube dysfunction – conductive loss without pain or fever.

Issue 1: Left-sided hearing loss/tinnitus  
• Assessment – Conductive vs sensorineural etiology undifferentiated; priority is direct visualization of ear canal and tympanic membrane.  
• Plan:  
  – Book in-person GP appointment within 4–5 days for otoscopy and possible microsuction/ear-syringing if wax seen.  
  – If ear canal clear, proceed with further evaluation (audiometry ± ENT referral).  
  – Provide patient education leaflet on tinnitus (link placed in chart).  
  – Advise patient to avoid cotton-bud insertion.  
  – Safety-net: return earlier if pain, discharge, worsening dizziness, sudden hearing loss, or other concerns.

Issue 2: Mild intermittent disequilibrium  
• Assessment – Likely secondary to same ear process; currently mild and non-disabling.  
• Plan: Monitor; escalate if vertigo, nausea, or neurological signs develop.

General plan items  
• Follow-up: Face-to-face visit as above; video review sooner if new/worsening symptoms.  
• Administrative: Doctor to send message to admin team and include support line number for scheduling.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements – No formal medication list, allergy verification, vital signs, or social history (smoking/alcohol/occupational noise) recorded.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts – None noted.  
● Transcript quality – Clear audio; minor conversational interruptions but clinically adequate.
